scenes.title: Iron Age farmstead at Llandough
scenes.narration: Excavations in 1978–79 at the separate Llandough Roman Villa site identified earlier Iron Age occupation. A curvilinear feature and postholes may represent a round hut; associated pottery is in a late Iron Age tradition. This is evidence for early occupation at Llandough, not evidence that a round hut stood on the Great House Farm parcel.

evidence.title: Heneb HER GGAT00768s — Llandough Roman Villa (Iron Age farmstead / possible round hut)
Coflein NPRN 400051 — Roman Villa Site, Llandough; excavation in 1979

scenes.known: Heneb's record for the separate Llandough Roman Villa site describes an Iron Age farmstead and a possible round hut, represented by a curvilinear feature and postholes. The pottery indicates a pre-Conquest tradition, but the record does not establish an exact date of c. 200 BC or show that the hut stood on Great House Farm itself.

scenes.title: Medieval occupation
scenes.narration: In 1962–63 E. J. Beare reports pottery of the 12th to 14th centuries on the slope north-east of the house. The Royal Commission classes the house as sub-medieval, probably 17th century, possibly with a medieval core.

scenes.title: The lordship of the manor
scenes.narration: Llandough belongs to Tewkesbury Abbey until the Dissolution of 1536–39. Cardiff Records states that in 1543 Henry VIII granted the manor to Lord Clynton and Say and Robert Turwitt, and that by 1545 it was held by Sir George Herbert. The Western Mail letter says the Herberts held the lordship until the Earl of Bute bought it in 1793; Cardiff Records places William Hurst and others in the account from 1767. The same 1974 newspaper record identifies Mary Williams's family as occupying the manorial home since 1667. That occupation and the lordship are separate from the farmhouse freehold. The family's case is that the Williamses were virtual freeholders under the 1877 bargain while quarrying continued, and that Parcel A's freehold passed to them in 1928 when quarrying ended.

evidence.title: Western Mail, 'Grievous loss' (1974 letter giving manorial descent and the Williams occupation)

scenes.received: The lord of the manor owned the farm.
received_words: The 1974 newspaper records the Williams family’s occupation of the manorial home; occupation is a separate matter from the lordship and the freehold.
scenes.known: Lordship of a manor and ownership of the farmhouse parcel are separate interests. The 1974 newspaper records the Williams family’s occupation of the manorial home since 1667. The family’s title case is not occupation alone: it is that the 1877 bargain entitled the Williamses to Parcel A’s freehold when quarrying ended, identified by Mary as 1928, when the final rent was paid. On that account, the Williamses were virtual freeholders while the quarrying arrangement ran and became freeholders in 1928. The 1877 deed and final receipt have not been located, so the 1928 transfer remains the family’s asserted title history rather than a fact determined by the 1974 newspaper or a court. The manorial sources also differ over 1767–1793; the Herbert estate papers have not yet been checked.
ledger: Lordship of the manor: Sir George Herbert (by 1545) and his family

scenes.title: A 1,000-year lease of Cydwin
scenes.narration: The National Library of Wales catalogue describes a lease for 1,000 years dated 20 June 1547 from Sir George Herbert of Swansea to Edmund Vaughan of a farm called Cydwin in the manor of Llandough; the record names fields. This long leasehold interest predates the later Bute estate narrative. The affirmative Cedwyn thesis asks whether those named fields belong to the older Cydfin/Ty Mawr holding later catalogued as a 107-acre farm, and how that interest passed from the Herbert/Vaughan line into subsequent estate records. The instrument and field boundaries must be examined before the lease can be equated with the whole Great House site.

scenes.title: The Vaughans
scenes.narration: From the mid-16th to the late 18th century the Vaughan family hold Great House as the chief freehold farm of the parish. The lordship of the manor is a separate interest, held over the same period by the Herberts.

scenes.received: One chain of owners: the Herberts, then the Vaughans, then Bute.
scenes.known: Two separate lines. The lordship of the manor: Tewkesbury Abbey, the Crown, the Herberts from 1545, Bute from 1793. The ownership of the farm: a freehold within the manor, held by the Vaughans until the late 18th century and by Bute from the early 19th. How the farm passed from the Vaughans to Bute is not yet documented. Parcel A's title descends from the farm freehold, not from the lordship.

scenes.title: The Williams family at Great House
scenes.narration: Mary Williams's c.1974 statement says her family had lived and farmed at Great House since 1667. A 1974 newspaper report also attributes to her a claim that her family first acquired Tŷ Mawr around that date. The affirmative Cedwyn thesis treats 1667 as the opening of the family's own estate history and tests that claim against the Cydwin/Cydfin lease and farm-name records. The surviving statement and press report support the Buckler case; a 1667 conveyance has not yet been identified.
scenes.received: Tenant farmers who lived on someone else's land.
received_words: The estate's description of the family, repeated in every later account.
scenes.known: Mary's statement and the 1974 press report support the Buckler case for a connection with Great House from 1667 and treat it as a lineage claim, not a passing tenancy. The affirmative reconstruction now connects that claim to the older Cydwin/Cydfin/Ty Mawr lease records and asks whether later labels of tenancy concealed a longer-standing family interest. The surviving items do not themselves constitute a 1667 conveyance; the deed chain must be reconstructed from the leases, estate accounts, plans and the 1877/1928 evidence.

scenes.title: Vaughan assigns the Cydwin lease
scenes.narration: The National Library of Wales catalogues an assignment dated 13 February 1739/40 by Edmond Vaughan of Llandough to Thomas Mathews of Llandaf of the 1,000-year Cydwin lease originally granted in 1547, for £1,066 13s. 4d. This is a documented transfer in the older lease chain and a concrete route for tracing who held the interest before Bute's later estate records. The next step is to match the named fields and follow subsequent assignments, rentals and conveyances into the Cydfin/Ty Mawr farm and the later parcels.

scenes.title: The Bute Estate
scenes.narration: The historical account places Bute's acquisition of the lordship of Llandough in 1793 and its acquisition of the Great House freehold in the early 19th century; the manorial courts of Llandough and Leckwith were held at the house. The missing control point is the instrument that carried the farm freehold from the Vaughan line into Bute's estate. The 1547 Cydwin lease, its 1739/40 assignment, and the D 219 record of Cydfin or Ty Mawr leases give the affirmative reconstruction a named chain to investigate alongside the manor's later ownership. A manorial interest, a long lease, and a farm freehold must be mapped separately before the later corporate titles can be treated as the originating chain for every parcel.

scenes.title: A Williams estate bequest to Bute: tracing the land
scenes.narration: The National Library of Wales catalogue lists the 1870 will of William Evans Williams of Pwllypant as bequeathing his real and personal estate to the Marquis of Bute, and separately catalogues papers about his real and personal estate. The affirmative title inquiry is parcel-specific: did any land he owned, benefited from, or had let through Bute connect to the 33-acre Llandough Limeworks block or Great House Farm? The will's headline bequest does not identify those acres by itself. The family's research also points to a Clock Tower dispute and newspaper coverage said to complicate the relationship between Williams and Bute; the precise contemporary reports and wording must be located before using that dispute as proof of motive. Estate schedules, title deeds, rent books and the 1876–1912 limeworks accounts are the route to answer the question.

scenes.title: The limeworks
scenes.narration: The Wiki's archive lead identifies about 33 acres used by the Llandough Limeworks from 1876 to about 1912, with Bute papers D153/4–8 to be obtained and inspected. The block's precise boundaries and title line remain to be matched to the 1877 plan and the estate schedules. For the Cedwyn reconstruction, this is a critical parcel-control point: identify who owned the freehold, who granted the quarrying rights, who received rent, and whether all four descriptions refer to the same acres.

scenes.title: Division of the farm
scenes.narration: Mary Williams's statement records that in 1877 the Bute Estate sold the farmhouse, buildings and about 10 acres to Daniel Thomas, and kept about 9 acres. The Williamses remained as tenants of both. The deed is missing.

Anything Bute sells after 1877 can only be Parcel B. Her statement says the freehold of the house was to pass to the Williamses when quarrying ended. The deed is missing; the wiki notes that whether the 1877 deal was a sale or a quarry lease is still to be tested against the Bute papers.

scenes.known: The only record of the time so far that the water was cut off: Mrs Buckler's own claim in 1958, as the Western Mail reported it. It names the landlord, Western Ground Rents, not a council. Crichel Down (1954) was the national scandal over farmland the state kept after requisition; a minister resigned over it. "Nearly 10 years" would put the start around 1948–49 (an inference). Per Branwen Buckler (voice testimony, relayed by Sion Buckler, 19 October 2026), the council cut the water over bills it said were unpaid, which Mary (Nancy) Williams insisted had been paid; dairy cattle drowned in the River Ely trying to reach water, a baby daughter had to live elsewhere, and the matter was raised in Parliament. What cuts against that version: the 1958 report names Western Ground Rents, not a council or a water bill; no report of cattle drowning has been found; no Commons or Lords debate or written answer has been found for 1946–92 (committee proceedings and MPs' letters are not searchable this way); and Dŵr Cymru's 2026 replies speak of a disconnection in the 1980s, so there may have been two cut-offs. scenes.title: Amalgamation of titles
scenes.narration: On 2 February 1987, while the appeal is pending, an application is made to amalgamate WA240304 (the separately registered farmhouse and garden) into WA231076 (the larger field title). The affirmative 'synthetic estate' question is whether a title originating in the Bute-to-WGR field chain was joined to a separately registered house title without the older Cydwin/Cydfin and Williams/Thomas chain being traced through the underlying instruments. The amalgamation records a registration event; its file, the 1877 documents, and the 1938 and 1969 conveyances must be read together to reconstruct the title's provenance.

The decisive exercise is to compare the first-registration files and the operative 1877, 1938 and 1969 instruments against the plans and schedules. scenes.narration: 1916 to 1987: a tenancy, two possession orders, three tenancy offers, licence letters, a conveyance, two registrations and an amalgamation.

evidence.title: The Two Parcels — the title test
BP Properties Ltd v Buckler [1987] EWCA Civ 2
Legal Review — Fraud, Land and Human Rights

scenes.received: A landlord and its successors recovered their farm from tenants who stayed on without paying, and the courts confirmed it.
scenes.known: Parcel A was the family's from 1928, and by possession from 1940. It was never shown to belong to Western Ground Rents or BP. A synthetic single farm was described in 1916; six attempts (1949, 1955, 1959, 1962, 1965, 1974) treated Mary's occupation as permissive; the woodland and the land to the south were taken; the 1975 conveyance and 1983 registration gave the synthetic Parcel A a deed and a title; the 1987 amalgamation folded it into Parcel B. The courts decided possession and never decided ownership. Possession can be awarded without ownership being tried, and land can be registered without a rival claim being decided. Neither decides the older title.
